DZR Is Back As Drift: The Minna Reminds Us Who Carries the Torch of Stylish SPD-Compatible Sneakers
24 photos
Photo: Drift Sports
If you ride a bike regularly, the chances that you encounter tarmac, gravel, trails, mud, and dust, are very high, sometimes, even in the same day. But you probably want to look decent enough to still grab a coffee with the crew before or after the ride, not to mention avoiding sounding like you’re walking around on horseshoes.
That leaves most all-round riders choosing the commonly encountered two-bolt SPD-compatible sneaker, offered by numerous brands these days. But it wasn’t always like this. Back in the day, I can remember going out for a ride in the middle of the Arizona desert and having to stay in my damn boots all day. The first thing I wanted to do was take them off at the first chance I got, and often did.
Photo: Drift Sports So, back in 2010, DZR (Drift Zone Racing) arrived on the scene , and sought to change all, and if I may, by God, they succeeded; DZR had entered the market by offering the first SPD-compatible sneaker and ones that looked hella good too, even setting a trend. Modern times list countless brands that provide what they feel is the true all-rounder shoe for cyclists.
The goal was to create a shoe that could handle being taken on trails just as much as it could be seen cranking it out on asphalt, and once they managed to show the world the ‘middle ground’ well, the rest is history.
But, after 14 years of providing “stylish” all-round footwear for cyclists, DZR decided to take a bit of a break, a break where they went back to the drawing board to reimagine the next generation of SPD kicks.
Well, they came back and not just with a redesigned lineup of pumps, but also, under a new name: Drift. The reemergence happened in April 2026, and since then, two pairs of kicks have been made available under the Drift name: the Arc, the one that brought them back on the market, and the Minna. The latter is the more affordable of the bunch and the ones that remind us of most of the former DZR shoes.
Photo: Drift Sports The Minna is a model that DZR ran with for several years, and I've added a few images to the gallery so that you can compare and contrast the generations.
Now, Drift continues the tradition that put them on the map in the first place, building shoes from the ground up by hand and doing so in limited numbers or “ small batches .”
The upper to the Minna is made with textile and suede upper while the outsole is good old rubber, with the two materials holding a reinforced toe cap in place. The shank is a stiff, composite one, helping you drive all your power into your pedals and supporting the cleat.
Yet one of the most important traits of the fresh Minna is the waterproof lining integrated into the shoe. This is an essential feature if you’re looking to ride on without worrying about the terrain you’re riding through or, if you’re walking your steed, where you step. Did I mention no longer needing to bring extra pairs of socks along on the rides or trudging it out with pruned toes that eventually turn into blisters?
Photo: Drift Sports Clearly, there are some limits to how waterproof a shoe can be, and stepping into a puddle up to your ankle is bound to push those limits, but Drift does mention that their shoes have been tested in wet trail conditions and even “ steady rain ” to ensure you’re not playing around on a mini slip-and-slide in your shoes.
Ventilation is also part of the story here and holes are visible over the toes and along the sides. I’m so curious to see how these babies perform because Drift recently approached us and asked if we’d like to give them a run; my answer was a clear “Yes!” This means we will be reviewing these kicks soon, and hopefully, while riding a very exciting new beast from a brand that I can’t mention just yet; I signed an NDA.
On the underside of the Minna we can also spot a change in comparison to previous generations. The older models had a continuous tread design from toe to heel, but for the new Minna, I noticed the tip of the soles have an angled surface, helping provide crucial grip when stepping on anything with limited and minimal space; they’re “ optimized for high traction on slick trails, pump tracks, and city streets .”
Photo: Drift Sports The recessed cleat continues to provide the same all-round use, suitable for clipping in but also stepping onto a classic pedal if you bought the shoes first and will have to wait till next month to buy the pedals.
Tracks to adjust your cleat are there, and covers are sure to also be on the menu (the Arc has them), even though Drift’s website doesn’t make a mention of the latter; I’ll check in with them and update the article once we have an answer.
Oh, and if you are looking for a starting point on the whole pedal journey, Drift has a little text on their website that compares three pedal pairs on the market and scores them. Have a look.
That’s for some of the technical side of the story, but one trait that borders on technical and aesthetics is the lace cover that the new Minna has in store; I don’t see it on the older models, and since I've never tested them, I don’t know how previous generations felt with loose laces or the Velcro straps.
Photo: Drift Sports But, the latest Minna has that integrated cover that neatly clicks into the tongue, and from what I can see, keeping your laces tucked in and free from your drivetrain. They also give the shoe a slightly skate-shoe-like look. Clean.
Speaking of looks, Shane Rattazzi, Drift Co-Founder and CEO, states that, “ The Minna respects our heritage in the SPD-compatible sneaker category with modern textile and suede blends to offer a more relaxed, versatile fit for everyday progression on and off the mountain ,” and the low-top look clearly contributes to even being able to wear these babies to a job interview, as long as they’re not filthy with mud.
As for the price for a pair of these babies, Drift mentions a rate of $190 (€170) for a pair of Minnas in any of the four colors.
Is the new Minna the perfect all-round SPD shoe? I’d say it depends on the wearer, but if we consider that this crew is THE godfather of this style of kicks, there should be no doubt that there’s something special going on here. We’re about to find out.
